COVID-19 Impact & Recovery
October 2023 Update
Damian Betebenner & Adam VanIwaarden — Center for Assessment

Utah State Board of Education
October 3rd, 2023

Background
Introductory Concepts and Terminology

COVID-19 Pandemic
• The COVID-19 Pandemic led to, arguably, the largest educational disruption in
 the history of the United States.
• Two-and-a-half years into the pandemic and the impacts of the pandemic are still
 being felt.
• The pandemic impacted students academically, emotionally, physically, and
 financially.
• In this overview, we focus address three things:
 • Academic Impact: What is it and what was happened to students in Utah?
 • Academic Recovery: What is it and what is happening to students in Utah
 currently?
 • Now What?: How can impact and recovery data be leveraged to help
 students going forward? ROI and other evidence-based investigations of
 what is working.

What is Academic Impact?
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functioned/
 functions as an “academic headwind”, impeding (in general)
 the academic progress of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
 ▪ They slow one’s rate of progress (speedometer)
 ▪ And by slowing one’s rate of progress, less distance is traveled (odometer).
• In education, these two impediments manifest as:
 ▪ Decrease in student growth (i.e., decrease in velocity = deceleration).
 ▪ Decrease in student attainment.

 4

Learning acceleration/deceleration
• Summarization of assessment data (either for diagnostic or
 accountability purposes) emphasizes two types of data results: Status
 (i.e., student attainment) and Growth (i.e., student academic progress)
• With the pandemic, the emphasis has changed to look at the
 academic impact
• Impact is synonymous with declaration
• Recovery is synonymous with acceleration
 ▪ Deceleration, by definition, is the change in velocity (i.e., a decrease in growth)
 ▪ Acceleration, by definition, is the change in velocity (i.e., increase in growth
▪ To understand whether and the extent to which recovery is occurring,
 one must understand the magnitude of impact.

 5

Assessment Data
• We investigated the impacts of the pandemic across two time frames:
 • Impact: Spring 2020 through Summer 2021
 • Recovery Year 1: Fall 2021 through Summer 2022
 • Recovery Year 2: Fall 2022 through Summer 2023
• To investigate the impact & recovery, we utilized RISE State Summative
 Assessment Data
 • Impact: RISE Spring 2019 to Spring 2021 (RISE testing canceled in
 2020)
 • Recovery Year 1: RISE Spring 2021 to Spring 2022
 • Recovery Year 2: RISE Spring 2022 to Spring 2023

 6

Assessment Data
• We investigated academic impact by using two complementary
 analyses:
 • Change in attainment (odometer): Equi-percentile scale score
 change (all grades)
 • Change in growth (speedometer): Baseline referenced student
 growth percentile (SGP) change (grades for which growth is
 calculated)

• The expectation is that education disruptions impacted instruction which in turn impacted
 (slowed down) student learning.
• RISE assessment data spring 2019 and 2021 was utilized to examine impact.

Overall Impact
• ELA
 • Decreases in the percent proficient ranged from upper single digits in lower grades to
 lower single digits in higher grades.
 • Median (baseline) SGPs ranged from lower 40s (lower grades) to mid 40s (higher grades)
 • Impacts were categorized as moderate
• Mathematics
 • Decreases in percent proficient were in mid to upper single digits.
 • Median (baseline) SGP decreases ranged from the upper single digits to lower double
 digits.
 • Impacts were categorized as moderate to large.
• Moderate impacts, under ideal circumstances can be made up in a year whereas large to
 severe impacts likely require multiple years of above-average (pre-pandemic) growth to
 recover to where students would have been had the pandemic not occurred.

Recovery Year 1
From Fall 2021 to Summer 2022
RISE: Spring 2021 and Spring 2022 Assessments

Recovery Phase
• During the 2021-2022 academic year, schooling returned to normal for most
 students.
• The hope was that a return to normal would lead to recovery of the academic
 losses incurred by students.
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic, to make up for
 those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above normal in order to catch up
 for those losses.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine whether recovery is occurring:
 • RISE data from 2021 and 2022
• We try to distinguish between: Recovery, Stabilization, Continued Deterioration

Two Types of Recovery: System & Student
• We elaborate on the results from the recovery analyses in two ways:
 • System level recovery: Is the education system supporting rates
 of learning that are comparable to what it was prior to the
 pandemic?
 • Student level recovery: Are student attaining at levels that are
 comparable to what they were prior to the pandemic.
• Previously, we focused mostly on system level impact: examining
 rates of learning in 2021 compared to those prior to the pandemic.
• We continue system level analyses but add additional focus in on
 student level recovery.
 22

 • Comparison of 2019 and 2022 same grade student growth: We examine

 utilizing coefficient matrices derived from pre-pandemic cohorts of students.
• Student level recovery
 • Comparison of 2019 to 2022 same grade attainment: We examine equi-
 percentile change in attainment for 2019 students and 2023 students.

Overall Recovery
• Analysis of 2022 RISE and ACCESS data indicates many trends in Utah
 to be happy about.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration was at least at the
 level of stabilization and, in many cases, could be considered genuine
 recovery.
• Compared to a dozen other states where the Center conducted these
 analyses, Utah comes out as the best in terms of pandemic recovery.
• Results from the 2023 data will be critical to assess whether these
 exemplary rates of learning (beyond what the state experience pre-
 COVID) are being maintained.

Now What
Leveraging Assessment Data to Help Students Overcome COVID-19 Academic Impacts

Exemplar Schools: Impact & Recovery
• Original discussions about examining ROI were redirected to examine Return on
 Activities:
 • Identify outlier schools in terms of impact/recovery.
 • Investigate whether activities (or lack thereof) could potentially be responsible
 for the school’s outlier status.
 • For schools with plausible activities leading to exemplary recovery, investigate
 links to relevant investment/funding.
• Step 1 is to find these outlier schools.
• We investigated schools along two dimensions:
 • Academic Impact (2019 to 2021 decrease in student learning)
 • Academic Recovery (2021 to 2022 increase in student learning relative to pre-
 pandemic 2018-2019 learning)

Exemplar Schools: Impact & Recovery
• As can be seen, Utah and its schools experienced a largely positive 2021-2022
• We’ve created Excel spreadsheets with the identified schools to help to sort
 through the many potential criteria to use to select exemplar schools
• As we discussed in Portsmouth, there was some concern that of low motivation
 leading to poor results. To examine we filtered on students with very low to very
 high and very high to very low growth.
 • Filtering out these students led to non-appreciable changes to the impact-
 recovery examinations of schools.
Questions
